newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels confirm Tuesday talks with government.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels confirm Tuesday talks with government.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 72 VIP hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima confirmed on Monday they planned to restart face-to-face talks with the Peruvian government Tuesday.

"The Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) manifests its total willingness to start conversations on Tuesday," rebel spokesman Nestor Cerpa Cartolini said in a three-point statement read over walkie-talkie from within the besieged compound.

But the rebel leader warned that resuming the direct talks that have been on hold since late December would not necessarily lead to a solution of the 55-day crisis unless the government addressed their demands.
"The beginning of the talks does not necessarily mean the beginning of the solution to the conflict," Cerpa said.
It was not clear how the two sides had reached an agreement to hold talks.
The rebels' principal demand for the release of some 400 jailed comrades, which they have maintained since storming the diplomatic mansion Dec. 17, was irrevocable, Cerpa added.
President Alberto Fujimori, who announced in London on Sunday fresh talks were scheduled for Tuesday, has refused to consider this demand.
Cerpa also said the rebels were as "determined to face a peaceful or military solution with the same conviction" as they had started the 55-day siege.

He said the 15 heavily armed rebels inside the residence were unbowed by what he dubbed as Fujimori's "veiled threat," claiming the president had said "if the conversations fail it would be a step towards the use of force."

Fujimori said in London Tuesday's talks would be between government negotiator Domingo Palermo and Cerpa's No. 2, Roli Rojas, known by his nom de guerre "El Arabe" (The Arab). Cerpa made no reference to who would represent the rebels at the negotiating table.

The rebels originally took more than 500 hostages during a lavish cocktail party but have freed most of them. The remaining 72 captives in the mined and booby-trapped residence include two Peruvian ministers, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors, about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen and Fujimori's brother.
